analysis.one_liner: Bans online ads targeted at people using their personal data.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or floor vote in the House and died when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have prohibited advertisers and the companies that deliver ads (like ad exchanges and social media platforms) from targeting ads at individuals using personal information such as browsing history, communications content, or data purchased from brokers. It would have kept contextual ads — ads matched to the page you are looking at, or to your general location — while banning profiling of individuals. The Federal Trade Commission, state attorneys general, and individuals could have enforced it, and it would have barred forced arbitration for violations.
analysis.who_benefits: Internet users. Today, companies track what people browse, search, and communicate and use that data to profile them and target ads. The bill would have ended that individual-level profiling, including profiling based on race, ethnicity, religion, sex, or disability, and given individuals the right to sue violators in court instead of being forced into arbitration [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits advertisers and ad facilitators from targeting ads using personal information such as browsing history, inferred data, or the contents of communications [S2] [S3].
Bars targeting based on information identifying someone as a member of a protected class, including race, religion, sex, and disability [S2] [S3].
Allows enforcement by the FTC, state attorneys general, and individuals, with statutory damages of $100–$5,000 per violation and invalidation of pre-dispute arbitration agreements [S3].
Permits non-invasive alternatives to continue, such as contextual ads shown next to content a person is already viewing and ads based on broad geographic location [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The online advertising industry: platforms and ad-tech companies would lose the personalization that lets them charge premium prices for precisely targeted ads, and advertisers — from national brands to small businesses — would lose the ability to reach specific customers. Free, ad-funded services could see revenue fall as ad prices decline, and some advertisers would face higher costs reaching customers through broader channels.

drawbacks.text: Targeted advertising is a primary way small businesses reach potential customers affordably; a broad ban would force them onto more expensive or less precise channels, and critics argued the ban goes far beyond the most harmful uses of data [S3].
Many free online services and publications are funded by ad revenue; a large drop in ad effectiveness could reduce that funding and shift costs to users or subscriptions [S3].
The private right of action with per-violation statutory damages and no forced arbitration could generate substantial litigation against companies for technical violations [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core tradeoff is real: ending individual-level ad profiling would curtail a mass data-harvesting system that most people never meaningfully consented to, including profiling by protected class. The cost is that targeted ads also fund much of the free internet and help small businesses find customers, so an outright ban would have real economic side effects. An honest reading is that the bill's consumer-protection goal was strong but its design was aggressive, going further than narrower privacy proposals that focus on opt-in consent and data minimization.

outcome.mechanism: The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its consumer protection subcommittee, where it sat with no hearing, markup, or floor vote until the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Anna Eshoo introduced the bill on January 18, 2022, with Reps. Schakowsky and Rush as original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day [S3] [S5].
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Consumer Protection and Commerce; no further action was ever recorded [S5].
It drew five cosponsors, all House Democrats, and no Republicans; the committee never marked it up and the House never voted on it before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S1] [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The digital advertising industry and the large platforms whose revenue depends on data-driven targeting kept their business model intact, since no restriction was enacted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Online ad platforms and data brokers

sides.party_line_note: Every cosponsor was a House Democrat (5 of 213); no Republican signed on, so the bill's support was entirely one-party and thin.

industries.industry: Digital advertising platforms and ad-tech companies
industries.note: Their core business is collecting personal data and selling precisely targeted ads; the bill would have banned that practice outright, including the sale of individual targeting lists. Their interest in defeating the bill ran directly against the privacy interests of the people they profile [S2] [S3].
Advertisers would have been barred from targeting based on data purchased from other people, cutting off a major market for brokers' profiles of individuals [S3].

They would lose the precision of targeted outreach and likely pay more to reach customers, but they would also stop competing inside an ad system that profiles their customers' race, religion, and health status.

Contextual advertising remains allowed under the bill, but the shift away from targeted ads could lower ad revenue for free content and services, pressuring them toward subscriptions or paywalls [S2] [S3].
